verses.1:
Al-Mizan presents this Meccan sūrah as centred on the Prophet’s mission as a warner bearing revelation and calling to God’s oneness (tawḥīd) and sincere worship. It first portrays the deniers’ haughtiness, division, obstruction of the Prophet, and baseless allegations; it then enjoins the Prophet’s patience, recalls earlier servants of God, contrasts the Godfearing with evildoers, and culminates in proclaiming tawḥīd and the Fire decreed for Iblīs and those who follow him after his refusal to prostrate before Adam.

In “Ṣād. By the Qur’an, full of remembrance (dhikr), the rejectors are in vainglory (ʿizzah) and schism (shiqāq),” dhikr denotes remembrance of God, His uniqueness, and the consequent truths of resurrection and prophethood. ʿIzzah is their disdainful haughtiness, while shiqāq is dissension or factionalism. The oath resembles other Qur’anic oaths and is not grammatically conjoined to the following verse. Its stated point is that their pride prevents their acceptance of the Prophet, as it did earlier peoples; its fuller sense, God knows best, is: by the Qur’an containing remembrance, the Prophet is among the warners, and those who deny him oppose and refuse to follow it. The commentary sets aside many proposed grammatical interpretations as unsupported by the text.

The destruction of earlier qurūn—peoples of particular eras—warns the deniers that previous communities received messengers, rejected their warnings, and cried out only when punishment had arrived. Their cry may be an admission of wrongdoing or an appeal for God’s help, but then no postponement or escape remained.

The idolaters were astonished that a human warner arose from among themselves, since they disdained a human messenger. Their charge that he was a lying sorcerer means that, unable to produce anything like the Qur’an, they called him a sorcerer and accused him of fabricating both the Qur’an and its claimed divine truths. Their question about making all gods one God expresses amazement at his denial of divinity to their alleged gods and his declaration that Allah alone is God. Jaʿala concerns their false religious assertions, not a literal transformation of things, and ʿujāb intensifies the sense of something extraordinarily strange.

The noblemen’s call to persist patiently in worshipping their gods suggests that they had jointly sought a conciliatory settlement with the Prophet but, after he would not yield, urged one another—or perhaps the masses—to remain attached to their gods despite what they regarded as his disparagement of them. Their statement, “This is what is desired,” most directly alleges that he invented prophethood to seek leadership. Other readings—that his steadfastness is admirable, that this is a fate imposed by Time, or that patience is itself desirable—are weak and do not suit the text.

By “the latest religions” (al-millah al-ākhirah), the deniers mean the religions of recent generations and their contemporaries: tawḥīd is, in their view, not the religion of their time but an invented lie. The proposal that this specifically means Christianity, on the basis of Christian trinitarian belief, is refuted by the text, particularly because Christianity had not taken root among the Meccan polytheists.

Their question, “Has the Reminder been revealed to one of us?” expresses distaste that Muḥammad rather than they should receive revelation and denies that he possesses a quality warranting divine selection. Their words arise not from an honest lack of proof but from doubt about the Qur’an: attachment to falsehood and inherited custom blinds them to its miraculous signs. Their arrogance will not permit confession of its truth until they taste punishment, after which they will taste nothing else.

The disjunctive questions in verses 9–10 refute their objection to the Prophet’s selection. They neither possess the treasuries of their Lord’s mercy nor control whom He appoints as messenger; God alone, being mighty and abundantly giving, distributes His special mercy as He wills. Nor do they rule the heavens, earth, and what lies between them. If they did, they should ascend by whatever means they can and prevent revelation from descending upon a man on God’s earth; the command exposes their incapacity.

They are a paltry, forsaken host, despite their boasts: the indefiniteness of jundun, the particle mā, and the distant hunālika emphasize their insignificance. They are counted among the factions that denied messengers and assembled against them, and are therefore called defeated even before their defeat, having earned punishment.

The peoples of Nūh, ʿĀd, Pharaoh, Thamūd, Lūṭ, and Shuʿayb—the dwellers of the wood (aṣḥāb al-aykah)—likewise denied the messengers and deserved the retribution that overtook and destroyed them. Pharaoh’s epithet dhū al-awtād means “the lord of spikes” or tent-poles; reports variously connect it with posts in his amusement grounds, his staking and torturing prisoners, or the soldiers supporting his rule, with no basis for preferring one explanation.

The present deniers await only one devastating blast, after which there will be neither return nor even a brief delay. Although some exegetes take this blast to be the Day of Resurrection because Muḥammad’s people were supposedly spared worldly punishment until then, the literal wording of the Qur’anic verses suggests otherwise. Finally, their demand that their qiṭṭ—their lot or destiny—be hastened before the Day of Account mocks both the coming of that Day and the promise of their punishment.

verses.3: Al-Mizan explains that qurūn are peoples of particular eras. Earlier communities received messengers and warnings but denied them, like these deniers; when punishment came, they cried either in admission of their wrongdoing or for God’s help, but the time for postponement or escape (manāṣ) had passed.
verses.4: Al-Mizan explains that the idolaters marvelled that a human warner had arisen from among their own people, since they disdained a human messenger. Calling the Prophet a lying sorcerer, they accused him of fabricating the Qur’an and its divine truths; the charge of sorcery reflects their inability to produce anything like the Qur’an.
verses.5: Al-Mizan takes the deniers’ rhetorical question as their astonished conclusion: the Prophet has declared their alleged gods devoid of divinity and Allah the sole God. The verb jaʿala concerns a false religious assertion, not a physical alteration, and ʿujāb is an intensified term for something extraordinarily strange.
verses.6: Al-Mizan reads the noblemen as having cooperated to confront the Prophet’s call to monotheism and rejection of their gods. After seeking conciliation and finding him immovable, they went about urging one another—or, less likely, the masses—to persist in worshipping their gods despite what they saw as his disparagement of them. “This is what is desired” most directly means that they alleged he had fabricated a prophetic mission to gain leadership. Alternative readings—that his steadfastness was admirable, that events were a fate imposed by Time, or that patience itself was desirable—are weak and ill-suited to the text.
verses.7: Al-Mizan explains “the latest religions” (al-millah al-ākhirah) as the religions of recent generations and of the deniers’ contemporaries. They mean that tawḥīd is not the religion of their age but an invented lie. The interpretation that the phrase specifically means Christianity, based on Christian trinitarian belief, is refuted by the text, especially because Christianity had not taken root among the Meccan polytheists.
verses.8: Al-Mizan says their question, “Has the Reminder been revealed to one of us?” conveys distaste that Muḥammad, rather than they, was chosen for revelation and denies that he possessed a quality warranting divine selection. Their speech stems not from hidden or inadequate proofs of his prophethood but from doubt in the Qur’an: attachment to falsehood and inherited custom blinded them to its miraculous signs. Their arrogance will not let them acknowledge its truth until they taste divine punishment, after which they will taste nothing else.
verses.9: Al-Mizan reads the disjunctive question as a refutation: the deniers do not possess the treasuries of their Lord’s mercy, so they cannot prevent Him from appointing whom He knows best as messenger or from bestowing special mercy upon whomever He wills. The closing names stress that God alone is mighty and inviolable in divine affairs and abundantly gives; it is not for them to withhold His mercy.
verses.10: Al-Mizan explains that the disjunctive command to ascend exposes the deniers’ inability. If they truly ruled the heavens, earth, and what lies between them, they should ascend by whatever means—such as stairs or a ladder—they can and prevent revelation from descending upon a man on God’s earth.
verses.11: Al-Mizan calls them a tiny, contemptible, forsaken host. The indefinite jundun, the particle mā, and the distant hunālika all underscore their insignificance despite their boasting. They belong to the factions that denied messengers and assembled against them, and thus earned punishment; they are called defeated even before their eventual defeat.
verses.12: Al-Mizan identifies the dwellers of the wood (aṣḥāb al-aykah) as Shuʿayb’s people and presents all the listed peoples as factions that denied the messengers and deserved the retribution that came near and destroyed them. Pharaoh’s epithet dhū al-awtād means the lord of spikes or tent-poles. It has been explained by posts in his amusement grounds, his torturing prisoners by staking them down, or the soldiers supporting his rule, but no evidence permits preference among these or other views.

verses.15: Al-Mizan explains that the deniers await only one blast that will destroy them, leaving neither return nor even a scant delay. Though some exegetes identify it with the Day of Resurrection because Muḥammad’s people were supposedly spared worldly punishment until then, the literal sense of the Qur’anic verses suggests otherwise.
verses.16: Al-Mizan explains qiṭṭ as one’s lot or destiny. By demanding that their punishment be hastened before the Day of Account, the deniers mock both the reality of that Day and the promise of punishment.
verses.17: Al-Mizan explains dhā al-ayd as “possessing power.” David’s power appeared in the force of his glorification, with which mountains and birds glorified God, as well as in his kingship, extensive knowledge, prowess in war, and killing of Goliath (Jālūt). Awwāb, an intensive form of awb, means that he continually turned back to his Lord.
verses.18: Al-Mizan takes maʿahu as qualifying yusabbiḥna: God made the mountains glorify Him together with David. Although a prepositional phrase normally follows its verb, its preceding position here suggests that the mountains imitated David’s glorification. By contrast, the usual placement in (21:79) emphasizes God’s inspiring the mountains and birds to praise with David, while (34:10) uses maʿahu in yet another position. ʿAshī and ishrāq mean evening and morning. Innā introduces an explanation: this verse and those following expound David’s power in glorification, kingdom, and knowledge, and his continual turning to God.
verses.19:
Al-Mizan explains maḥshūratan as the birds’ hurried assembling: God made them congregate and praise with David. “All turning to Him” continues the description of the mountains and birds; their unceasing glorification is itself a turning toward God. Although lahu could possibly refer to David, this is unlikely.

God inspires their praise independently of David, since all things truly glorify Him, not merely as though they did so. The mountains and birds are singled out because their praise was united with David’s and could actually be heard by people.
verses.20:
Al-Mizan explains “We strengthened his kingdom” as a figurative “making firm”: David’s rule and judgment were bolstered through such means as power, wealth, soldiers, and sound administration. Ḥikmah is certain and correct comprehension of what benefits the human being and advances human perfection, rather than specifically prophethood, the Psalms, or knowledge of religious law.

Faṣl al-khiṭāb is the ability to analyze another’s words and distinguish truth from falsehood, especially in adjudicating between litigants. The interpretation that it means concise speech, or merely the phrase ammā baʿad, is less fitting, since the following verse concerns litigants.
verses.21: Al-Mizan explains khaṣm as people engaged in a dispute, and tasawwarū as climbing to the top of a high wall. The miḥrāb is understood as an upper room or alcove. The rhetorical question draws attention to the unusual account and invites its continuation: Muḥammad is asked whether he has heard of disputants who climbed the walls of David’s sanctuary.
verses.22:
Al-Mizan explains that the second idh specifies how the litigants scaled the sanctuary: they entered David’s room by climbing its walls and barging in rather than using the normal entrance, which alarmed him. Fazaʿ is shrinking from or recoiling against a fearsome thing; unlike khashyah, it belongs to action taken against an apparent threat, as does khawf. It is therefore not blameworthy but can be praiseworthy insofar as it helps one recognize and guard against danger. David’s fazaʿ does not conflict with prophethood or with prophets fearing none but God.

The men reassured David after startling him. They describe themselves as two opposing parties, one having wronged the other, and ask him to judge truly, without tushṭiṭ—tyranny or injustice—and to guide them to an equitable resolution.
verses.23:
Al-Mizan explains that one disputant calls a member of the opposing side his brother and alleges that he owns ninety-nine ewes while the speaker owns one. Naʿjah means a female sheep; akfilnīhā asks that the ewe be placed under the other man’s custody and authority, and “he overpowered me in speech” means that he prevailed over him verbally.

The plural wording concerning their scaling the wall and coming to David does not prove that the smallest plural is two. Although the disputers are described in the dual and the speaker says “my brother,” each side could have had several supporters, or others may have joined the initially two-sided dispute.
verses.24:
Al-Mizan holds that David may have hastened to judge from the lone ewe owner’s emotionally compelling account before hearing the other side, though the owner of the ninety-nine ewes might have had a right to the ewe. David’s statement means, with an oath, that the man had wronged him by asking him to add his ewe to the other’s flock. His further observation concerns khulaṭāʾ, associates who intermingle their property: they commonly wrong one another, except the believers who act righteously, and these are few.

Ẓanna here means that David knew, rather than merely suspected, that the event was a divine test, since he sought forgiveness, fell in bowing, and anāb—returned to God in repentance and sincerity. The prevalent narrated view is that the litigants were angels. Their extraordinary entry, David’s recognition of a test, and the ensuing command to judge truly and not follow whim all support this: the episode alerted and strengthened him in rule and judgment.

The commentary considers it highly likely that the entire occurrence was a dream or vision manifested by the angels, not a physical event involving actual litigants or sheep. Since religious responsibility pertains to the visible material realm, David’s slip in such a vision incurred no formal responsibility. His repentance is comparable to Adam’s repentance for his slip before earthly religious responsibility, and both are expressly called caliphs.

Some exegetes instead regard the litigants as human. On that reading, David’s words are a provisional evaluation: the claimant was wronged unless the other produced proof of entitlement. This preserves what reason and narrations require—that prophets are protected from both major and minor sins—and avoids contradicting God’s prior gift to David of sound judgment and clear understanding of speech.
verses.25: Al-Mizan explains zulfā as a lofty station and prestige, and maʾāb as return. Their indefiniteness conveys the grandeur of David’s nearness to God and beautiful return.
verses.26:
Al-Mizan reads these words as spoken to David when God forgave him. His khalīfah is a divinely appointed authority, like the caliph mentioned in (2:30). Because a caliph succeeds by reflecting the successor’s attributes and acts, God’s caliph on earth must intend, act, judge, and rule according to God’s decree and remain on His path.

The link between making David caliph and commanding him to judge truly shows that this was an actual, realized caliphate, not an honorary or merely potential title: God brought David’s rule to fruition and gave him authority to judge. Interpretations that make him only a successor to earlier prophets, or treat judging as simply an office transmitted by any caliph, require unwarranted elaboration and lack textual support.

The prohibition against following whim concerns judgment: whim diverts from truth, which is God’s path. The command is genuinely addressed to David, even though it also warns other authorities. Infallibility does not remove free choice; commands and prohibitions must still apply to the infallible, or obedience, disobedience, and protection from disobedience would lose their meaning.

Straying through disobedience is inseparable from forgetting the Day of Accounting—that is, failing to remain vigilant about it—and this forgetfulness leads to severe punishment.
verses.27:
Al-Mizan presents this as the first of two arguments for the Resurrection. The transient heavens, earth, and all between them must have a fixed, eternal end; otherwise their creation would be bāṭil, devoid of any real goal, which cannot be attributed to the wise God. Bāṭil may possibly bear the broader sense of purposeless play, as in creation not being made for amusement.

The interpretation that the verse merely warns against following whim because the world was created for tawḥīd and obedience to divine law does not accord with the following contrast between the righteous and corrupt. The deniers imagine a purposeless world with no Day of Accounting in which all matters are finally disclosed; hence their punishment in the Fire.
verses.28:
Al-Mizan presents this as the second argument for the Resurrection. Human perfection is attained by moving from potentiality to actuality in knowledge and action. Sound fiṭrah directs people to belief in truth and righteous action, which also reform human society. Thus believers who act righteously are the perfected reverent (muttaqūn), whereas those whose corrupt beliefs and deeds spread corruption are the wicked (fujjār): imperfect losers who fall short of true humanity. This distinction necessarily bears on a wholesome or otherwise livelihood.

In the present world, however, material causes operate equally for believers and disbelievers, perfected and imperfect alike: work supported by the necessary means brings prosperity, and its absence brings wretchedness. If life ended there, with no further realm suited to distinguish the two groups, God would fail to restore rights and treat claims justly; indeed, equal treatment regardless of desert would conflict with divine justice. The verse does not deny their shared worldly circumstances, but contrasts believers who act righteously with those who do not, and the reverent with the wicked. The preceding argument is rational, while this one is dialectical.
verses.29: Al-Mizan explains that the blessed Book was sent down as a complete whole before its gradual revelation, since pondering and reflecting upon it presuppose an available book rather than scattered leaves. The pronoun in “so that they may ponder” encompasses all human beings. The Book overflows with goodness and blessing, especially for those who reflect and are guided by it; alternatively, its arguments and proofs guide those with understanding to the truth.
verses.30: Al-Mizan explains that God bestowed Solomon upon David as his son, calling him an excellent servant who often turned to God.
verses.31: Al-Mizan, citing Majmaʿ al-Bayān, explains that ʿashiyy is the latter part of the day after midday, opposite ghadāh. Ṣāfināt are horses standing on three legs with one hoof raised, while jiyād denotes swift, racing steeds.
verses.32:
Al-Mizan explains that Solomon preferred the horses, called khayr by the Arabs, to the remembrance of his Lord—that is, prayer. Although some exegetes take khayr as immense wealth, the horses are the intended meaning. His love for them was for God’s sake, since they could be prepared for jihad; thus one act of worship distracted him from the more important worship of prayer until sunset.

“It was hidden in the veil” most suitably refers to the sun setting behind the horizon, a reading supported by the preceding mention of eventide. Some instead say the horses vanished into the distance, but there is no Qur’anic or narrated evidence that Solomon then ordered the horses, rather than the sun, to be brought back.

The preferred interpretation of “Bring it back to me” is that Solomon commanded the angels to return the sun so that he could pray on time; he and those with him then wiped their legs and necks for ablution and prayed. Some narrations from the Imams of Ahl al-Bayt relate this view. A secondary interpretation is that he recalled and stroked the horses’ legs and necks, dedicating them to God’s way in recompense for his distraction.

The commentary rejects the claim that he slew the horses by severing their legs and necks. Such punishment would not befit a prophet: the horses bore no fault for his missed prayer and were likely another’s property. A report ascribed to the Prophet through Ubayy ibn Kaʿb is invoked for this claim, along with the assertion that horses were sacrificed in their religious law, but the commentary calls this baseless, since no narration establishes such a practice. Solomon’s distraction was not wanton; the first interpretation therefore best accords with the text, and the second is preferable if it is not adopted.

verses.34:
Al-Mizan explains that jasad is a body without a soul. It rejects the view that the body on Solomon’s throne was Solomon himself, gravely ill and slumped like a corpse: this requires an omitted pronoun and an ineloquent, non-literal reading of “We placed.”

The most suitable interpretation among those based on differing narrations is that it was a young boy whose soul God took and whose body was left against the throne. Solomon’s subsequent turning to God and plea for forgiveness indicate that the boy was his son, in whom he had placed hopes for the way of God. God thus reminded Solomon to leave matters in His hands.
verses.35: Al-Mizan holds that Solomon’s plea for forgiveness and for an unparalleled kingdom follows his turning to God after the body was placed on the throne. Its lack of wāw makes it flow as the answer to what he said when he turned to God. His request was not miserly: he sought a special kingdom uniquely his, not the removal of others’ kingdoms or the prevention of others from seeking a distinctive kingdom.
verses.36: Al-Mizan regards this as the answer to Solomon’s prayer and an explanation of his incomparable kingdom: he was granted dominion over the winds and jinn. Rukhāʾ functions adverbially, meaning that the winds blew softly and compliantly wherever Solomon directed, not that the winds themselves were intrinsically soft; this would conflict with their description elsewhere as gusting. It is nevertheless possible that God made some winds tame and others tempestuous according to Solomon’s wishes.
verses.37: Al-Mizan explains that Solomon was given control over shayāṭīn: land-jinn who built and sea-jinn who worked in the sea and extracted pearls and the like.
verses.38: Al-Mizan explains that aṣfād are iron shackles, and that Solomon controlled other jinn who were bound together in chains.
verses.39: Al-Mizan explains that the kingdom was God’s exclusive gift to Solomon, requiring nothing in return. “Without reckoning” seemingly means that it was endless: whether he gave freely or withheld it, his kingdom would not diminish. Other exegetes take the phrase to mean that he would not be held accountable for it on the Day of Resurrection, or that he should give without expecting a return.
verses.40: He enjoyed nearness to God and an excellent return.
verses.41:
Al-Mizan explains that Job’s call to his Lord was an implicit plea for healing and the removal of his affliction; humility kept him from stating the request explicitly, while “His Lord” shows his distress. Nūṣb means exhaustion, and the phrase “when he called out to his Lord” identifies the intended referent of “Our servant,” Job.

“Toil and torment” concern the calamities in Job’s health and family, as clarified by his prayer, “Affliction (ḍarr) has befallen me, and You are the most merciful of the merciful!” (21:83). Neither this sūrah nor Sūrah al-Anbiyāʾ says that he lost wealth; that comes from narrations. The verse attributes the affliction to Satan, and narrations likewise establish this causal relation. Satanic and natural causation do not conflict, since they operate at different levels of existence.

The commentary argues that Satan can affect people in this way, just as defiling practices are described as wrought by Satan (5:90), and Moses calls a killing “the work of Satan” (28:15). Apart from narrations, the affliction may instead be understood as Satan’s whispering among people, leading them to shun, slander, and mock Job because of his suffering.

Tafsīr al-Kashshāf rejects Satan’s power to torment prophets, maintaining that his authority extends only to whispering. Al-Mizan replies that prophetic and infallible sinlessness protects them from inward satanic misguidance, not from bodily or other external harm that does not entail misguidance. Joshua’s statement, “I forgot the fish, and the only one who made me forget to mention it was Satan” (18:63), illustrates this. Satan’s bodily harassment neither reaches prophets’ hearts nor escapes God’s will; it may serve such higher purposes as displaying their patience and turning to God, and nothing occurs without God’s permission.
verses.42: Al-Mizan takes the command, “Strike with your foot,” immediately after Job’s prayer as announcing its answer. It may have been addressed directly to Job, or may abbreviate that God answered him by telling him to strike with his foot. The command specifically indicates that Job could not stand or walk. God healed his feet, caused a spring to flow there, and commanded him to wash and drink, thereby curing his whole body inwardly and outwardly; narrations support this interpretation. The verse leaves the intervening sequence unstated: Job struck with his foot, washed, drank, and was healed by God.
verses.43:
Al-Mizan reports narrations that Job’s trials included the death of all his family except his wife; God then revived them and gave him others like them. Another view is that they had merely been separated from him during his hardship and were reunited after his healing, by which time their descendants made their number comparable to the former one.

The phrase “as a mercy from Us and a reminder to those with understanding” expresses the purpose of what God did for Job: it was a mercy from Him and a reminder for people of understanding to contemplate.
verses.44:
Al-Mizan cites Majmaʿ al-Bayān that a ḍighth is a handful of straw, hay, twigs, branches, or the like. Job had sworn, if healed, to give his wife one hundred lashes because she had upset him. Once healed, God instructed him to take a bundle of rushes, one stalk for each lash, and strike with it so that he could fulfill his oath. The verse only alludes to his wife and the cause of his oath, omitting them out of respect for him.

“We found him patient” means that God found Job patient amid His trials, including the loss of health, family, and wealth. The commentary considers it more likely that this explains why he was called God’s servant in the preceding verse. “A most excellent servant! He ever turned [to Us]” is praise of him.
verses.45:
Al-Mizan explains that Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are praised as men of might (ayd, from yad, “hand”) and insight (abṣār, from baṣar, “vision”). Hands are rightly used for righteous deeds that extend goodness to creation, and eyes for recognizing the path of safety, discerning truth, and avoiding falsehood.

Thus, “hands and eyesight” metaphorically denotes their firmness in obeying God and benefiting others, together with their insight into truth in faith and action. This is synthesized in the description that God made them Imams who guide by His command, revealed to them the doing of good, prayer, and alms, and that they served Him (21:71–73): divine command and revelation concern their insight, while doing good, prayer, and alms concern their might. A reported interpretation likewise understands the verse as referring to their strength and insight in worship.
verses.46:
Al-Mizan explains aklaṣnāhum bi-khāliṣatin as God’s complete purification of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob through the trait of remembering the final abode. Khāliṣah, “purification,” stands grammatically in place of the noun it describes, and bi- denotes causality. The abode (dār) is the hereafter.

The verse may explain “men of might and insight,” “Our servants,” or “And remember” in the preceding verse, though the first is preferable. Whoever is wholly occupied with the hereafter and nearness to the Lord necessarily gains complete cognizance before Him: such a person sees the truths of faith, understands the path of worship, and is saved from absorption in worldly materiality and adornment. This contrasts with one who turns from God’s reminder and seeks only worldly life (53:29).

Some exegetes instead take dār to mean the worldly life and understand the purification as their enduring good repute, citing (19:49–50). The commentary prefers the meaning of the final abode.
verses.47: Al-Mizan states that being among the elect (al-muṣṭafīn) entails complete submission to God, and that the verse alludes to Allah’s choosing of Adam, Noah, the descendants of Abraham, and the descendants of ʿImrān above the nations (3:33). Akhyār is said to be the plural of khayr, “good,” the opposite of evil; alternatively, it may be the plural of khayyir or of khayr.
verses.48:
Al-Mizan considers the meaning of the verse about Ishmael, Elisha, and Dhū al-Kifl being among the finest to be clear.

It then notes that the Qur’an says only that Job was severely tried in his health and children, after which God relieved and healed him and restored his family and their like as mercy and a reminder to the servants (21:83–84). Sūrah al-Anʿām includes him among Abraham’s prophetic descendants and praises them (6:84–90), while Sūrah Ṣād calls him patient, the best of servants, and ever-turning towards God (38:44).
verses.49: Al-Mizan notes that some exegetes take “This is a reminder” to refer to the previously mentioned prophets: their enduring honor and praise, with the reverent denoting either those prophets specifically or all reverent people. It finds it more apparent, however, that it refers to the Qur’an and its remembering contents, especially because dhikr earlier denotes the Qur’an in By the Qur’an, full of remembrance (wal-qurʾān dhī al-dhikr,38:31). The chapter then turns to the hereafter’s reward for the reverent and punishment for transgressors. Their maʾāb is the place to which they return, and its indefiniteness conveys its enormity.
verses.50: Al-Mizan explains the gardens as an everlasting abode and life. Their opened doors figuratively mean that nothing obstructs the delights prepared for their inhabitants; some exegetes take this to mean they need not wait or knock, while others say the doors open and close without keys or locks.
verses.51: Al-Mizan explains that the inhabitants recline luxuriously, in a manner signifying honor and nobility. They may call for abundant fruit and drink, which will be brought without any effort or need to rise and obtain it.
verses.52: Al-Mizan explains that the reverent will have female consorts of modest gaze (qāṣirat al-ṭarf), either devoted solely to their partners or described figuratively as coy and coquettish. Atrāb means peers (aqrān): they may be alike to their partners in age or handsomeness, or reflect their partners’ light and splendor, becoming more beautiful as it increases.
verses.53: Al-Mizan says that the promise concerns the gardens and their delights. The shift to direct address conveys nearness and honor, adding spiritual blessings to the manifest, materialized ones.
verses.54: Al-Mizan explains nafād as perishing, being extinguished, or running out. The verse concludes the preceding description by affirming that this divine sustenance never ends.
verses.55: Al-Mizan takes “Thus” to refer to the reverent’s happy end, though it may also function as an ism fiʿl, meaning “Take this.” In contrast, the transgressors have an evil journey’s end.
verses.56: Al-Mizan explains that yaṣlawnahā means entering Hell and enduring its heat or effects. According to Majmaʿ al-Bayān, mihād is a laid-out bed, hence something prepared; the verse and the next describe what awaits the transgressors.
verses.57: Al-Mizan explains ḥamīm as scorching and, according to Majmaʿ al-Bayān, ghassāq as fetid, stinking pus, though it has also been explained otherwise. The wording and its emphatic order indicate that the condemned will be compelled, unwillingly, to drink this boiling ooze and pus.
verses.58: Al-Mizan explains shakl as a thing resembling another and of the same sort, and azwāj as types (anwāʿ) or categories (aqsām). Thus there are diverse further drinks like the boiling and oozing fluids, which they must drink.
verses.59: Al-Mizan reads these verses as foretelling a quarrel in the Fire between vicious leaders and their followers. Addressing the leaders, “This troop” indicates that both parties descend together as a battalion, with muqtaḥim denoting a forceful storming in. The leaders deny their followers any welcome, and the followers return the denial, blame the leaders for bringing them to the Fire, and ask God to punish twice whoever offered them this fate. “Twice” (ḍiʿfan) means two of the same, hence a double portion of torment. The leaders’ response is not stated here; Sūrah al-Ṣāffāt reports them as saying, “No, you were not believers. And we had no authority over you; you were a rebellious people (37:29–30).”

verses.62: Al-Mizan understands the speakers to be the dwellers of Hell. They seek men they had considered vicious, but cannot find them in the Fire because those men are in Paradise.
verses.63: Al-Mizan explains their question as uncertainty whether they had erred in mocking people who then attained salvation, or whether their eyes had simply failed to see those people despite their being in the Fire.
verses.64: Al-Mizan says that dhālik refers to the Hell-dwellers’ disputes and establishes their wrangling as an undoubted fact. Their bickering manifests the propensity for feuding and fighting that lay within them during earthly life.
verses.65:
Al-Mizan explains that the Prophet is commanded to declare both that his sole mission is warning, not the pursuit of wealth or rank, and that God alone is divine. “There is no god but Allah” denies that anything else has a rightful claim to worship. The dispute between Islam and shirk is not over God’s divinity, but over whether worship belongs exclusively to Him.

The divine names establish this exclusivity. As the One and the Subduer (al-wāḥid, al-qahhār), God is unlike anything else, infinitely perfect, absolutely needless, and the giver of existence and its effects to every other being. All things therefore depend on, obey, and are humbled before Him. This inherent submission is the reality of servitude and worship: even if worship of another existent were supposed, it would in truth be worship of God, since that thing has neither independent being nor control. God alone is truly worthy of worship.

His lordship over the heavens, the earth, and all between them supplies a further proof. The world has one undivided order, indicating one administering divinity; creation and governance are inseparable. Since God creates and administers all things, including His foes, worship—which expresses the relation of servitude to the governor and bestower of blessing—must be directed to Him alone. This phrase may also elaborate “the One, the Subduer.”

As the Mighty, none can compel or restrain God, while everything else is meek before Him; worship, being an expression of meekness, befits only Him. As the Forgiving, He alone removes the remoteness caused by sins, grants mercy, and brings servants to the honored abode of the hereafter. Thus He is worshipped in hope of forgiveness. Possibly, “the Mighty, the Forgiving” also indicates why the Prophet calls people to tawḥīd: God’s unconquerable might and forgiveness show Him to be the true deity.

verses.67: Al-Mizan takes “it” to refer to the proclamation of God’s oneness in “there is no god but Allah… (38:66).” Some exegetes instead identify it with the Qur’an, the tremendous tidings (nabaʾ ʿaẓīm), which they consider more fitting with the surrounding verses and the Prophet’s knowledge of the exalted assembly through the Qur’an. Others identify it with the Day of Judgment, but this is the least likely view.
verses.68: Al-Mizan takes “it” to refer to the proclamation of God’s oneness in “there is no god but Allah… (38:66).” Some exegetes instead identify it with the Qur’an, the tremendous tidings (nabaʾ ʿaẓīm), which they consider more fitting with the surrounding verses and the Prophet’s knowledge of the exalted assembly through the Qur’an. verses.69: Al-Mizan explains that the exalted assembly (al-malaʾ al-aʿlā) is an assembly of angels, apparently referring to their exchange when God announced that He would place a caliph on earth. The verse means that the Prophet knew nothing of this dispute among the angels on high until God revealed it in His book; he is a warner who follows revelation.
verses.70: Al-Mizan says that this reinforces “I am but a warner” (38:65) and accounts for the Prophet’s lack of prior knowledge of the angels’ dispute. His knowledge does not arise from himself, but from revelation, and he receives revelation concerning divine warning.
verses.71:
Al-Mizan holds that this verse and the next are not part of the speech commanded to the Prophet in verses 38:65–70, as indicated by “your Lord,” addressed singularly to him. They return to the time of the angels’ deliberation on high. “When” either refers to the time of their dispute or implies “Recall when your Lord said to the angels”; God’s announcement that He would place a caliph on earth and His announcement that He would create a mortal from clay belong to the same time denoted by idh. Thus the verse recalls the occasion of the dispute.

Some exegetes make the verse an explanation of the dispute and construct an extended dialogue among God, the angels, and Iblīs, with divine speech and angelic speech mediated through an angel so that the disagreement occurs among angels themselves. Al-Mizan rejects this construction as wholly unsupported by the text.

Bashar means the human being, particularly the bodily and outward human form; it may be singular or plural. The descriptions of human origin as clay (ṭīn), dust (turāb), moulded mud, and dry clay like pottery refer to differing states of the original material from which the human being was made.
verses.72: Al-Mizan explains that “fashioned” (sawwaytuhu) means equipping the human being with limbs and completing the human form. Breathing “part of My spirit” means giving him a living human spirit, while “My” expresses honor. The command to “fall” orders the angels to prostrate because God had fashioned the human being and breathed His spirit into him.
verses.73: Al-Mizan takes the verse in its most direct sense: every angel prostrated, without exception.
verses.74: Al-Mizan explains that Iblīs, unlike the angels, refused to prostrate out of pride and was a faithless ingrate.
verses.75:
Al-Mizan explains that being created “with My two hands” expresses a special, honored relation between God and the human being, like the breathing of God’s spirit into him. The use of two hands conveys God’s full care and attention in creation, as people use both hands for what matters to them. Some exegetes understand “hand” as power and the two hands as emphasis; this interpretation also occurs in narrations. Other proposed meanings—worldly and otherworldly blessings, body and soul, or the attributes of grandeur and beauty (jalāl and jamāl)—have no textual evidence.

“Are you too proud or too exalted (min al-ʿālīn)?” censures Iblīs for refusing prostration: was he arrogant, or did he regard himself as too lofty to receive the command? Some exegetes infer that the ʿālīn are created beings so absorbed in their Lord that they perceive nothing but Him. Others make ʿālīn mean arrogance, so that the question asks whether Iblīs became arrogant only after the command or had always been so; Al-Mizan rejects this because the verse asks why he is arrogant. The view that the ʿālīn are heavenly angels exempt from the command, unlike earthly angels, is likewise unsupported, since the verse implies that the angels generally were commanded to prostrate.
verses.76: Al-Mizan says that Iblīs explains his refusal by claiming an innate superiority over Adam: he was created from fire, Adam from clay. His reply implies that a divine command should be obeyed only when it seems right to him, rather than simply because God commanded it. This rests on his refusal to accept God’s all-encompassing dominion. Such self-exemption from worship and divine rule is the root of sins: one judges disobedience preferable to the command and thereby turns away from it.
verses.77: Al-Mizan explains rajīm as “rejected” and yawm al-dīn as the Day of Resurrection. Whether the wording is “My curse” or “the curse,” the result is the same: along with the divine curse, the curse of angels and human beings is upon Iblīs. By God’s command he is truly outcast and banished from divine mercy.
verses.78: Al-Mizan explains rajīm as “rejected” and yawm al-dīn as the Day of Resurrection. Whether the wording is “My curse” or “the curse,” the result is the same: along with the divine curse, the curse of angels and human beings is upon Iblīs. verses.79: Al-Mizan notes that Iblīs asks for respite until the Day of Judgment, but God grants it only until “the known time” (yawm al-waqt al-maʿlūm). This is the final time of the world, before the Day of Judgment, when disobedience is no longer possible. “Day,” reinforced by waqt, denotes a period of time rather than necessarily a particular or solar day.

verses.82: Al-Mizan explains that the bi- in bi-ʿizzatika is an oath: Iblīs swears by God’s might that he will mislead everyone except God’s purified servants. These are those whose souls God has purified, beyond the reach of Satan or anyone else.
verses.83: Al-Mizan explains that the bi- in bi-ʿizzatika is an oath: Iblīs swears by God’s might that he will mislead everyone except God’s purified servants. These are those whose souls God has purified, beyond the reach of Satan or anyone else.
verses.84:
Al-Mizan takes this as God’s reply and irrevocable decree that Hell will be filled with Iblīs and his followers. “The truth” may mean either “I swear by the truth” or “My word is true”; in either case truth, repeated with the definite article, is opposed to falsehood. “The truth I speak” is parenthetical, stressing that God speaks only truth and refuting Iblīs’s claim of superiority or his implicit claim that the command to prostrate was wrongful.

The decree concerns shayāṭīn generally, including Iblīs, his descendants, and his tribe; their followers are the human beings who follow Iblīs.

verses.86: Al-Mizan says that this returns to the chapter’s governing theme: the Qur’an is a reminder and the Prophet is only a warner. It also answers the call to persist with false gods. The Prophet’s refusal of reward shows that he seeks neither wealth nor status, while his denial of being a pretender (mutakallif) means that he is not a charlatan who invents something and dresses it up as what it is not.
verses.87: Al-Mizan explains that the Qur’an is a reminder for all peoples, tribes, and nations, not for one group to the exclusion of another or something for which payment may be taken for reciting or teaching it.
verses.88: Al-Mizan explains that people will, after a time, come to know the truths announced by the Qur’an, including the Resurrection, Islam’s prevalence over other faiths, and other matters. Some exegetes limit the time to the Day of Judgment, death, or the Battle of Badr. It is also reasonable that several times are intended: the verse need not specify one day, since each kind of foretold matter becomes known in its own time.
